content: Pulmonary surfactant plays a critical role in the host defense mechanism against respiratory infections. In late preterm or term newborn infants, bacterial pneumonia frequently results in surfactant deficiency or dysfunction. This occurs because surfactant can become inactivated or undergo peroxidation during the course of the infection. Evidence from animal models of pneumonia and clinical case reports suggests that administering exogenous surfactant may provide therapeutic benefits to infants suffering from bacterial pneumonia. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of exogenous surfactant therapy on mortality rates and pulmonary complications in infants diagnosed with bacterial pneumonia. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the standard methodology of the Cochrane Collaboration. The databases searched included the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, The Cochrane Library 2011, Issue 6), MEDLINE (via Ovid SP, June 2011), EMBASE (via Ovid SP, 1980 to June 2011), and CINAHL Plus (via EBSCOHost, June 2011). The inclusion criteria for this review were limited to randomized and quasi-randomized trials that investigated surfactant replacement therapy in infants born at greater than 35 weeks of gestation who developed bacterial pneumonia within the first 28 days of life. The primary outcomes of interest were mortality, time to resolution of pneumonia, incidence of chronic lung disease, occurrence of pneumothoraces, and pulmonary hemorrhage. All studies identified during the search were assessed for eligibility based on predefined criteria. Data extraction was performed using RevMan 5 software (RevMan 2011), and the standard Cochrane methodology was applied to evaluate risk of bias, heterogeneity, treatment effects, missing data, and reporting bias. No studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified during the review process. Consequently, there is no evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to either support or refute the efficacy of exogenous surfactant therapy in late preterm and term infants with confirmed or suspected bacterial pneumonia. Further RCTs are necessary to address this clinical question.
